examples: The board finally accepted that the launch date had to move.
She accepts that nothing she says is going to change his mind.
Even his critics accept the basic finding.
I'll accept that I was wrong about the route, but not about the time.
The court accepted her account as accurate.
Nobody in the room accepted that the outage had lasted only six hours.
entries.русский: признать, принять — согласиться с тем, чему сопротивлялся; вины не подразумевает
entries.patterns: accept + that-clause · accept + noun phrase · accept + noun phrase + as + noun phrase / adjective · passive it is accepted that
entries.never: accept to do something — accept takes no to-infinitive in any of its senses, and ✗She accepted to help is the most persistent error made with this verb by speakers of French, Spanish, and Italian. Repairs: agreed to help, accepted the job, accepted that she had to help. Also accept me that — no personal object stands before the clause.
entries.reports: coming around to a proposition you had been resisting, usually after evidence or argument. Weaker than concede, which needs a specific point surrendered in a dispute, and it carries none of the fault that admit does — you can accept a fact that reflects on nobody.

examples: The mayor acknowledged that the city had missed the deadline.
She acknowledged receiving the letter but said she never opened it.
He acknowledged the mistake without apologizing for it.
The study acknowledges what the earlier work got right.
It is widely acknowledged that the original estimate was too low.
He acknowledged to the committee that no one had read the contract.
entries.русский: признать — официально подтвердить, что нечто так; самое нейтральное в ряду, без вины
entries.patterns: acknowledge + that-clause · acknowledge + -ing · acknowledge + noun phrase · acknowledge + noun phrase + as / to be · acknowledge + wh-clause · acknowledge + to sb + that-clause · passive it is acknowledged that
entries.never: acknowledge to do something and acknowledge me that — there is no to-infinitive after this verb, and the listener needs a preposition: ✓acknowledged to me that he was late, ✓acknowledged being late.
entries.spelling: American English writes acknowledgment, with no e before the -ment, on the same pattern as judgment. British English writes acknowledgement, keeping the e; that spelling is British, not an American variant, and it should not be copied into American work.
entries.reports: a formal admission that something is so. The lightest verb in the family — admit presupposes fault and confess presupposes guilt, but you can acknowledge a debt, a favor, or an email with nothing at stake.

examples: She admitted that she had never read the contract.
He admitted to me that the whole story was secondhand.
The airline admitted overbooking the flight.
Two of them admitted to falsifying the timesheets.
I'll admit it — I forgot the appointment completely.
He would never admit how much the repair actually cost.
Nobody admitted to being in the building after six.
entries.русский: признать, сознаться — уступить в том, что говорит против тебя; вина подразумевается
entries.patterns: admit + that-clause · admit + -ing · admit + to + -ing · admit + noun phrase · admit + to + noun phrase · admit + to sb + that-clause · admit + wh-clause · passive it is admitted that · (unrelated senses: admit + sb + to + noun phrase "let in"; admit + of + noun phrase "leave room for")
entries.never: admit to do something and admit to have done something — the complement is an -ing form or a that-clause, never an infinitive. ✗He admitted to take the money. ✗He admitted to have taken the money. ✓He admitted taking the money. ✓He admitted that he had taken the money. Also admit me that — the listener needs to: ✓admitted to me that.
entries.-ing or to + -ing: both are standard American and they mean the same thing; admitted taking it is a shade more written, admitted to taking it a shade more spoken. The to in the second is a preposition, which is precisely why no infinitive can follow it.
entries.spelling: the t doubles before a vowel — admitted, admitting — but not in admission.
entries.two other verbs in the same spelling: admit also means "let in" (She was admitted to the ward that night; British English drops the article — admitted to hospital) and, in formal writing, "leave room for" (The wording admits of no other reading). Neither reports speech, and the first is why admitted to has to be read twice: admitted to the clinic was let in, admitted to taking it owned up.
entries.reports: conceding something that counts against you. The fault is presupposed rather than asserted, which is why admitted is unfair attribution for a fact the speaker volunteered freely.
entries.see also: acknowledge, concede, confess, own up to, deny

examples: The historian allows that the letter may be a forgery.
I'll allow that the price was fair, given the market.
He allowed that he had been unfair to her.
Even the dissent allows that the statute is ambiguous.
She allowed as how the drive would take most of a day.
Critics generally allow that the early novels are the stronger ones.
entries.pronunciation note: the second syllable rhymes with now, not with low
entries.русский: признать, допустить — книжн., устар.: спокойно уступить пункт; обиходный глагол — concede
entries.register: formal and somewhat dated in this sense; the everyday allow is the permission verb
entries.patterns: allow + that-clause · allow + of + noun phrase (allows of no exception) · (in its unrelated permission sense: allow + sb + to-infinitive, allow + -ing, allow + noun phrase)
entries.never: in the concession sense, allow to do and allow -ing are both impossible — ✗I allow to be wrong, ✗I allow being wrong, ✓I allow that I was wrong. Also allow me that he was right: no personal object stands before the clause. Take care with allow + sb + to-infinitive, which is perfectly grammatical but is the other verb — I allow him to be right grants him permission and concedes nothing.
entries.two verbs in one spelling: The historian allows that the date may be wrong concedes a point; The landlord allows pets grants permission. The that-clause is the reliable signal — only the concession verb takes one.
entries.regional: allow as how survives in Southern and rural American speech (He allowed as how it might rain) and reads as dialect anywhere else. The complementizer as how has its own entry under conjunctions.
entries.reports: granting a point, in a register that now sounds bookish. Like concede it presupposes resistance — nothing gets allowed that was not first in doubt — but the surrender is calm rather than forced out. Choose it when the concession is being made in writing; concede is the everyday verb.

examples: She announced that she was leaving at the end of the month.
The district announced the closure by text at six in the morning.
He announced to the whole table that he had gotten the job.
They still haven't announced who won.
It was announced on Friday that the merger had fallen through.
My brother announced his engagement on a group call.
entries.русский: объявить, огласить — сделать нечто публичным и официальным
entries.type: reporting verb — public statement, often a revelation
entries.patterns: announce + that-clause · announce + noun phrase · announce + wh-clause · announce + noun phrase + to sb · announce + to sb + that-clause · passive it was announced that
entries.never: announce me the news and announce me that — announce never takes a bare indirect object, and the audience always goes into a to-phrase. ✗She announced us the results. ✓She announced the results to us. ✓She announced to us that the results were in. Also announce to do.
entries.word order: when there is both a listener and a clause, the to-phrase comes first: announced to the staff that the office was closing. Putting it last (✗announced that the office was closing to the staff) attaches it to the wrong verb and says something absurd.
entries.reports: making something public and official. Where reveal presupposes concealment and leak presupposes that the release was unauthorized, announce presupposes only that the speaker had the standing to say it.

examples: His accent betrayed him within about five words.
Her expression betrayed nothing at all.
The letter betrays the fact that he already knew about the sale.
He betrayed no surprise when the verdict was read out.
A pause on the line betrayed how bad the news was going to be.
She betrayed herself by asking about a detail nobody had told her.
entries.русский: выдать, невольно обнаружить — о голосе, лице, паузе: показать то, что скрывали
entries.patterns: betray + noun phrase · betray + the fact that · betray + wh-clause · betray + no / little + noun phrase · betray + oneself
entries.never: betray that he was nervous — the bare that-clause is dispreferred in careful writing; use a noun phrase or the the fact that bridge: ✓betrayed his nervousness, ✓betrayed the fact that he was nervous. Also betray to do, betray -ing, and betray me that.
entries.the subject is usually a sign, not a spe: a voice, a face, an accent, a pause. The person given away appears as the object: her voice betrayed her.
entries.reports: letting something show without meaning to. The other betray — turning on someone — is the same word, and the overlap is why this one always carries a faint suggestion that the revealer was on the wrong side of the secret.
entries.see also: give away, let slip, let on, reveal

examples: He blurted out that he had already accepted another offer.
She blurted the whole thing out before anyone could stop her.
Don't blurt out the ending — half of them haven't seen it.
I blurted out the first number that came into my head.
Someone in the back blurted out what everyone was thinking.
He blurted it out and then spent an hour apologizing for it.
"It wasn't me," he blurted out before anyone had even asked.
entries.русский: выпалить, ляпнуть — сказать сгоряча, не подумав, то, что собирался утаить
entries.patterns: blurt out + that-clause · blurt out + noun phrase · blurt + noun phrase + out · blurt out + wh-clause · blurt out + direct quotation
entries.never: blurt out to do, blurt out -ing, and blurt me out that. The particle also cannot follow a pronoun object: ✗blurted out it, ✓blurted it out.
entries.separable: a full noun phrase can sit on either side of the particle (blurted out the answer / blurted the answer out), but a pronoun must sit between the verb and the particle.
entries.reports: saying something suddenly and without thinking, usually something the speaker meant to hold back. Plain blurt exists, but blurt out is the ordinary American form.

examples: He came clean about the credit card debt.
She decided to come clean with her parents over dinner.
It took him a year to come clean about missing the deadline.
If you come clean now, this stays between us.
The company never came clean about how long the data had been exposed.
I'd rather come clean than keep patching the story.
entries.русский: признаться начистоту — разг.: наконец сказать правду после долгого сокрытия
entries.patterns: come clean (no complement) · come clean + about + noun phrase · come clean + about + -ing · come clean + with sb · come clean + to sb + about
entries.never: come clean that he had lied — the idiom takes no that-clause at all. Repairs: came clean about lying, admitted that he had lied. Also come clean to do and come clean the truth — there is no direct object either.
entries.fixed form: clean here is an adjective and never inflects — came clean, coming clean, never ✗came cleanly.
entries.reports: finally telling the truth after a stretch of concealment. It presupposes a prior lie or cover-up more strongly than admit does, and the tone is conversational throughout.
entries.see also: own up to, fess up, confess, admit

examples: He conceded that the first draft had been rushed.
She conceded the point but not the argument.
The senator conceded the race a little after midnight.
Even the study's authors concede that the sample was small.
She would not concede that any part of it had been her idea.
The company conceded two of the five claims and fought the rest.
He conceded to reporters that the campaign had run out of money.
entries.русский: уступить, признать — сдать пункт под давлением; предполагает предшествующий спор
entries.patterns: concede + that-clause · concede + noun phrase · concede + noun phrase + to sb · concede + to sb + that-clause · passive it is conceded that
entries.never: concede to do and concede me that — the listener needs to: ✓conceded to reporters that the race was over. The bare -ing that admit takes so easily is unnatural here: ✗conceded making a mistake, ✓conceded that he had made a mistake. The wh-clause is shaky too — He would not concede how much it had cost wants admit.
entries.reports: giving up a point under pressure, in an argument or a contest. What it presupposes is not fault but resistance — there has to have been a dispute for anything to be conceded. In journalism it is as loaded as admitted, and it should be used only when the resistance is on the record.

examples: He confessed to taking the cash out of the register.
She confessed that she had known about it for months.
Two suspects confessed within the first day.
I'll confess I've never actually finished the book.
He confessed his part in it to the auditors.
After six hours she still hadn't confessed.
entries.русский: сознаться, признаться в вине — в том, за что могут осудить или наказать
entries.patterns: confess + that-clause · confess + to + -ing · confess + to + noun phrase · confess + noun phrase · confess + noun phrase + to sb · confess + to sb · confess + to sb + that-clause · confess (no complement)
entries.never: confess to do — the to is a preposition, so no infinitive can follow it: ✗confessed to steal the car, ✓confessed to stealing the car. Also confess me that, which needs to: ✓confessed to her that. The bare -ing without to is possible but dispreferred — confessed to taking it beats confessed taking it.
entries.two things to can introduce: the offense or the audience. He confessed to the burglary names what he did; He confessed to the detective names who heard it. When a sentence needs both, one of them has to move — He confessed the burglary to the detective, or He confessed to the detective that he had done it.
entries.reports: admitting to something you can be blamed or punished for. Stronger than admit by exactly the distance between fault and guilt, and it keeps a religious and legal residue — you confess to a priest, to the police, or to a court. The weakened social use (I confess I've never read it) is a politeness formula and carries none of that.
entries.see also: admit, own up to, come clean, acknowledge

examples: He confided that the marriage had been over for years.
She confided in her roommate and in nobody else.
He confided his doubts to a colleague over lunch.
She confided to me that she had turned the offer down.
He has never confided in anyone about the diagnosis.
They confided in each other for thirty years.
entries.русский: поделиться по секрету, довериться — рассказать личное с условием, что не разгласят
entries.patterns: confide + that-clause · confide + in sb · confide + in sb + that-clause · confide + in sb + about + noun phrase · confide + noun phrase + to sb · confide + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: confide me that and confide me the news — the listener takes in or to, never a bare object. ✓confided in me that, ✓confided to me that, ✓confided her plans to me. Also confide to do and confide -ing.
entries.in or to: confide in someone names the relationship — trusting them as a rule; confide something to someone names one act of telling. She confides in her sister and She confided the news to her sister are both correct and mean different things.
entries.reports: telling something private on the understanding that it stays private. The secrecy is presupposed; the fault is not.
entries.see also: reveal, disclose, let on, divulge, volunteer

examples: Nobody at the table dared contradict him.
The second witness contradicted the first on every detail.
He contradicted himself twice in the same paragraph.
The lab results contradict the company's timeline.
She contradicted the official account within an hour of reading it.
I'm not trying to contradict you — I just remember it differently.
entries.русский: возразить, уличить в неправде — дополнение здесь лицо, а не утверждение (ср. deny)
entries.type: reporting verb — denial of someone else's statement
entries.patterns: contradict + sb · contradict + noun phrase · contradict + oneself · passive be contradicted by
entries.never: contradict that — no that-clause of any kind. ✗He contradicted that he had been there. Use deny for a speaker's denial about himself (He denied that he had been there), and contradict plus a noun phrase for the rejection of somebody else's statement (He contradicted her account). Also contradict to do, contradict -ing, and contradict me that.
entries.reports: saying that what someone else said is untrue. Alone among the denial verbs it takes a person as its object — you contradict her, but you deny the claim — and it needs a prior statement to work on: with nothing on the record, there is nothing to contradict.

entries.meaning: Only the first reports speech. They denied her access to the file reports no statement at all, and the two frames never blend — you cannot deny someone that something happened.
examples: She denied any knowledge of the payments.
He denied knowing the other driver.
The department denies that the recording was edited.
Ask him directly and he'll deny it.
Both companies denied having been contacted by regulators.
He never denied being at the party — only that he had stayed late.
entries.русский: отрицать — заявлять, что обвинение ложно; другое значение — «отказать кому-л. в чём-л.»
entries.patterns: deny + that-clause · deny + -ing · deny + having + past participle · deny + noun phrase · deny + it · passive it is denied that
entries.never: deny to do something — the commonest error made with this verb anywhere. ✗He denied to take the money. ✓He denied taking the money. ✓He denied that he had taken the money. There is no to-infinitive after deny in any sense, and no to + -ing either: ✗denied to taking it. Also deny me that he was there — no personal object stands before the clause.
entries.reports: asserting that a claim about you is false. The mirror image of admit, and it presupposes the same thing: that an accusation is already on the table.

examples: The campaign disavowed the ad within hours.
He disavowed any connection to the earlier filings.
The agency disavowed the report as unauthorized.
She has never disavowed the essay, even under pressure.
The party quietly disavowed its own platform from four years earlier.
Both founders disavowed the decision once it went public.
entries.русский: отмежеваться, отречься — книжн.: публично отвергнуть свою связь с чем-либо
entries.patterns: disavow + noun phrase · disavow + any / all + noun phrase · disavow + noun phrase + as + noun phrase / adjective · passive be disavowed by
entries.never: disavow that, disavow -ing, disavow to do, and disavow me sth. The verb takes a noun phrase and nothing else: ✗He disavowed that he had written it, ✓He disavowed the letter, ✓He denied writing it.
entries.reports: publicly cutting yourself off from something you are being associated with — a statement, a group, an ad, a decision. Where deny says the fact is untrue, disavow usually concedes the fact and rejects the connection.

examples: The seller disclaims any warranty beyond thirty days.
She disclaimed all credit for the idea.
The estate disclaimed an interest in the property.
He disclaimed responsibility for the numbers in the appendix.
The label disclaims liability for damage in transit.
Both parties disclaimed knowledge of the third contract.
entries.русский: снять с себя ответственность, отказаться от притязаний — юр., офиц.; ср. сущ. disclaimer
entries.patterns: disclaim + noun phrase · disclaim + all / any + noun phrase · passive be disclaimed
entries.never: disclaim that, disclaim -ing, disclaim to do, and disclaim me sth. The object is always a noun: ✗disclaimed that he was responsible, ✓disclaimed responsibility.
entries.reports: formally refusing responsibility, ownership, or credit. Narrower than deny: you deny a fact, but you disclaim a liability, a warranty, an interest, or a connection. The noun disclaimer is far commoner than the verb and is where most Americans meet the word.

examples: The company disclosed that two executives had sold stock in March.
He failed to disclose the payments on his ethics form.
She would not disclose how much the settlement was worth.
The filing discloses a second lawsuit in Ohio.
Nothing was disclosed to shareholders until after the vote.
Doctors must disclose any financial ties to the manufacturer.
The bank disclosed to regulators that the account had been open for years.
entries.русский: раскрыть, разгласить — офиц., юр.: сообщить то, что обязан был или мог не сообщать
entries.patterns: disclose + that-clause · disclose + noun phrase · disclose + wh-clause · disclose + noun phrase + to sb · disclose + to sb + that-clause · passive it was disclosed that
entries.never: disclose me the terms — no double object; the recipient takes to: ✓disclosed the terms to us. Also disclose to do, disclose -ing, and disclose me that.
entries.reports: making known something you had a duty or an option to keep quiet about. The same act as reveal, in the register of contracts, filings, and regulators — and it adds an obligation that reveal does not carry, which is why a company fails to disclose rather than fails to reveal.

entries.respell: dih-SPYOOT as a verb; the noun is usually /ˈdɪspjut/
examples: She disputes the charge on principle, not on the amount.
Nobody disputes that the building needs a new roof.
The union disputed the company's account of the meeting.
Historians still dispute whether the letter is genuine.
He disputed every line of the invoice.
The finding has been disputed by two other labs.
entries.русский: оспаривать — заявлять, что утверждение спорно, а не прямо ложное (ср. deny)
entries.patterns: dispute + that-clause · dispute + noun phrase · dispute + wh-clause · dispute + whether-clause · passive be disputed
entries.never: dispute to do, dispute -ing, and dispute me that. ✗He disputed having said it, ✓He disputed that he had said it, ✓He denied saying it.
entries.a negative habit: the that-clause version turns up under negation far more often than not — no one disputes that, nobody is disputing that, few would dispute that. That frame asserts something while appearing merely to report agreement, and a careful reader notices.
entries.reports: challenging a claim as wrong without necessarily denying it outright. Deny says it is false; dispute says it is contestable, which is how the same fact can be disputed by both sides at once.

examples: He would not divulge the source of the recording.
The office declined to divulge how many people had applied.
She divulged the terms to a reporter that evening.
Nothing was divulged before the embargo lifted.
Employees agree not to divulge anything covered by the contract.
He divulged that the buyer was a competitor.
She divulged to a colleague that the audit had already started.
entries.русский: разгласить, выдать — книжн.: сообщить то, что должно было остаться в тайне
entries.patterns: divulge + noun phrase · divulge + that-clause · divulge + wh-clause · divulge + noun phrase + to sb · divulge + to sb + that-clause · passive be divulged
entries.never: divulge me the details and divulge me that — no double object, and the recipient always takes to: ✓divulged the details to me, ✓divulged to me that. Also divulge to do and divulge -ing.
entries.a negative habit: divulge appears under refusal far more often than not — would not divulge, declined to divulge, without divulging. In a plain positive sentence it sounds arch, and reveal or disclose is usually the better verb there.
entries.reports: giving out information that was supposed to stay in. The most secretive of the revealing verbs, and the one that most clearly presupposes a confidence being broken.

examples: The investigation exposed a decade of falsified inspections.
He was exposed as the author of the anonymous memo.
The audit exposed the fact that nobody had signed off on the payments.
Her testimony exposed how the contracts were awarded.
A single email exposed the whole arrangement.
The documentary exposed conditions the company had denied for years.
entries.русский: разоблачить — вскрыть скрываемое, во вред тому, кого разоблачают
entries.patterns: expose + noun phrase · expose + noun phrase + as + noun phrase / adjective · expose + the fact that · expose + wh-clause · passive be exposed as
entries.never: expose that the reports were falsified — the bare that-clause is dispreferred in careful American writing. Repairs: revealed that the reports were falsified, exposed the falsified reports, exposed the fact that the reports were falsified. Also expose to do, expose -ing, and expose me that.
entries.reports: revealing something the subject was actively hiding, and revealing it against them. Reveal is neutral about whose interest is served; expose always serves the reader against the person exposed, which makes it a verdict as much as a report.

examples: Somebody needs to fess up about the dent in the door.
She fessed up to forgetting the appointment entirely.
He fessed up the second his mother asked.
Just fess up — everybody already knows.
Nobody fessed up to sending the email.
He fessed up to me about it a week later.
entries.русский: сознаться, повиниться — разг., амер.: усечённое от confess, о мелком проступке
entries.patterns: fess up (no complement) · fess up + to + noun phrase · fess up + to + -ing · fess up + about + noun phrase · fess up + to sb
entries.never: fess up that he took it — no that-clause; say fessed up to taking it, or move to plain admitted that he took it. Also fess up to do (the to is a preposition) and fess up the truth — there is no direct object.
entries.origin and range: a clipped American reshaping of confess. It belongs to conversation and to headlines that are being playful; in anything formal it is out of place.
entries.reports: owning up to something minor, with none of the gravity of confess. The tone is nearly always light — you fess up to eating the last slice, not to a felony.
entries.see also: own up to, come clean, admit, confess

examples: Don't give away the ending.
His accent gave him away before he finished the sentence.
She gave away the surprise a week early.
One glance at the schedule gave away what they were planning.
He gave the whole thing away by congratulating her too soon.
Nothing in the report gives away who wrote it.
entries.русский: выдать, проболтаться — нечаянно раскрыть тайну; тж. выдать концовку, заспойлерить
entries.patterns: give away + noun phrase · give + noun phrase + away · give + oneself + away · give away + the fact that · give away + wh-clause
entries.never: the particle cannot follow a pronoun — ✗gave away it, ✓gave it away. A bare that-clause is dispreferred too: ✗His face gave away that he knew, ✓His face gave away the fact that he knew, ✓His face gave him away. Also give away to do and give away -ing.
entries.other senses: the same phrasal verb means "donate" (gave away the furniture) and "escort a bride down the aisle." Only the revelation sense reports anything.
entries.reports: letting a secret out by accident, usually through a sign rather than a statement. Close to betray but plainer and far commoner in speech; it is also the ordinary verb for spoiling a plot.
entries.see also: betray, let slip, blurt out, spill

examples: I'll grant that the timing was unlucky.
She grants the point and moves straight past it.
Granted, nobody expected the road to be closed.
I'll grant you that much and no more.
He granted that the earlier version had been clearer.
Even granting that the data are old, the trend is hard to miss.
entries.pronunciation note: British English has the broad a, GRAHNT
entries.русский: признать, согласиться — уступить пункт мимоходом, обычно перед «но»
entries.patterns: grant + that-clause · grant + sb + that-clause · grant + noun phrase (grant the point) · grant + sb + noun phrase (I'll grant you that much) · granted (that) as a concessive opener · granting that in a participial phrase
entries.never: grant to do and grant -ing — ✗He granted to be wrong, ✗He granted being wrong, ✓He granted that he was wrong. Take care with grant + sb + noun phrase, which is two verbs at once: with a concessive object it is this one (I'll grant you that much, I'll grant you the point), but with a thing handed over it is the other grant (The court granted him bail), which reports no speech at all.
entries.reports: conceding a point graciously and usually in passing, on the way to disagreeing about something larger. It is almost always a step toward a but: I'll grant you the price is good, but the location is impossible.

examples: He hinted that there might be an opening on his team.
She hinted at a change in the schedule but wouldn't say more.
The manager hinted to us that the branch was closing.
He hinted heavily about what he wanted for his birthday.
Nothing in the memo even hints at a delay.
She hinted at leaving the firm and then said nothing for a year.
entries.русский: намекнуть — указать на что-то, не называя прямо; без злого умысла, ср. insinuate
entries.patterns: hint + that-clause · hint + at + noun phrase · hint + at + -ing · hint + about + noun phrase · hint + to sb + that-clause · hint + broadly / heavily
entries.never: hint his resignation — hint takes no direct object, and the thing hinted at needs at: ✓hinted at his resignation. Also hint me that → ✓hinted to me that, and hint to do.
entries.reports: pointing at something without saying it, and leaving the hearer to finish the job. It is neutral about motive, which is what separates it from insinuate — a hint can be kind; an insinuation cannot.

examples: She implied that the decision had already been made.
Nothing in the email implies any criticism of your team.
Are you implying that I made it up?
The policy implies a level of oversight that nobody actually provides.
He implied as much without ever quite saying it.
The wording implies that the deadline is negotiable.
entries.русский: подразумевать, давать понять — говорящий implies, слушающий infers (это не синонимы)
entries.patterns: imply + that-clause · imply + noun phrase · passive it is implied that
entries.never: imply me that — there is no bare personal object, and even the prepositional implied to me that is stiff where suggested to me that is ordinary. Also imply to do and imply -ing.
entries.imply or infer: the speaker implies; the listener infers. They are the two ends of one act, not synonyms, however often infer is used for imply in speech.
entries.reports: conveying something without stating it, so that the speaker can disown it later. Unlike hint, it need not be deliberate — a sentence can imply something its author never noticed.

examples: Early results indicate that turnout was higher than expected.
He indicated to the board that he would step down in June.
The report does not indicate who authorized the transfer.
Her silence indicated the answer well enough.
Nothing in the file indicates a second payment.
The witness indicated that she had seen the car twice.
entries.русский: указывать на, свидетельствовать — о данных; о человеке — обтекаемо дать понять
entries.patterns: indicate + that-clause · indicate + noun phrase · indicate + wh-clause · indicate + to sb + that-clause · passive it is indicated that
entries.never: indicate me that → ✓indicated to me that. Also indicate to do and indicate -ing.
entries.two uses: with a non-human subject it reports evidence (the data indicate that); with a human subject it is a bureaucratic hedge that reports speech while declining to quote it (he indicated that he would resign) — useful when the exact words are unavailable, and a dodge when the writer does not want to commit to them.
entries.reports: pointing toward a conclusion. More cautious than reveal, and unlike imply it is normally about evidence rather than intent.

examples: He insinuated that the reference letter had been written by a friend.
Nobody said it outright, but the piece insinuates a cover-up.
She insinuated to the committee that the data had been chosen after the fact.
What exactly are you insinuating?
The article insinuates far more than it can prove.
He spent an hour insinuating that the deal had been arranged in advance.
entries.русский: намекать со злым умыслом, инсинуировать — бросать тень, оставляя путь к отступлению
entries.patterns: insinuate + that-clause · insinuate + noun phrase (rare) · insinuate + to sb + that-clause · (in an unrelated sense: insinuate oneself into)
entries.never: insinuate me that → ✓insinuated to me that. Also insinuate to do and insinuate -ing.
entries.reports: implying something damaging while keeping it deniable. The judgment is baked in and cannot be switched off: to call a statement an insinuation is to accuse the speaker of bad faith. That is why the verb almost never appears in the first person — I'm implying nothing of the kind is a defense, but I insinuated that is nearly a confession.

examples: The ambassador intimated that the deadline could move.
She intimated to her editor that a second book was under way.
He intimated as much in his letter of resignation.
The chairman intimated that the vote would not be close.
Nothing was said directly, but the reply intimated a refusal.
He intimated that his support came with conditions.
entries.pronunciation note: the verb has three full syllables and ends in /eɪt/; the unrelated adjective is /ˈɪntɪmɪt/ · IN-tih-mit
entries.русский: дать понять, намекнуть — книжн.: глагол произносится /ˈɪntɪmeɪt/, не как прилагательное
entries.patterns: intimate + that-clause · intimate + noun phrase (rare) · intimate + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: intimate me that → ✓intimated to me that. Also intimate to do and intimate -ing.
entries.reports: hinting, one register above hint and without the malice of insinuate. It lives in written English and in reported diplomacy; in speech it reads as affected, and the pronunciation trap — saying it like the adjective — is why many writers leave it alone.

examples: Someone leaked the draft budget two days before the vote.
The memo was leaked to three outlets at once.
He leaked that the plant would close by summer.
Nobody has figured out who leaked it.
The findings were leaked before the study had been peer-reviewed.
She leaked the roster to a rival team's staff.
entries.русский: слить (информацию) — журн.: без разрешения передать сведения, обычно прессе
entries.patterns: leak + noun phrase · leak + noun phrase + to sb · leak + that-clause · passive be leaked to
entries.never: leak the reporter the memo — no double object; the recipient takes to: ✓leaked the memo to the reporter. Also leak to do and leak -ing.
entries.reports: releasing information deliberately and without authorization, usually to the press. The unauthorized part is the whole meaning — what an official body puts out is announced or disclosed, never leaked. The verb is neutral about whether the leaker was right to do it.

examples: She knew for weeks and never let on.
Don't let on that I told you.
He didn't let on how much the treatment had cost.
If she was disappointed, she didn't let on.
He let on to a couple of people that he was interviewing elsewhere.
Whatever you do, don't let on to your sister.
He never let on about the second interview.
entries.русский: подать вид, проговориться — разг., чаще с отрицанием: «и виду не подал»
entries.type: reporting verb — revelation, usually under negation
entries.patterns: let on + that-clause · let on + wh-clause · let on (no complement) · let on + about + noun phrase · let on + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: let on sb that → ✓let on to anyone that. Also let on to do, let on -ing, and no direct object: ✗He let on the secret, ✓He let the secret slip, ✓He let on that he knew.
entries.negative polarity: let on lives under negation — never let on, didn't let on, without letting on, don't let on. A plain positive (He let on that he knew) is grammatical but rare enough to sound slightly off unless a to-phrase follows.
entries.reports: allowing someone to find out what you know or feel, usually by failing to hide it. Let on leaks a state of mind; let slip leaks a fact.
entries.see also: let slip, give away, confide, betray

examples: He let slip that the offer had already been accepted.
She let it slip to a coworker and it was everywhere by noon.
Somebody let slip the date of the announcement.
He let slip a detail that only three people knew.
Try not to let anything slip before Friday.
She let slip to her brother that the house was going on the market.
entries.русский: проговориться, обронить — нечаянно выдать факт, часто сам того не заметив
entries.patterns: let slip + that-clause · let slip + noun phrase · let + noun phrase + slip · let + it + slip + that-clause · let slip + to sb + that-clause
entries.never: let slip to do, let slip -ing, and let slip me that → ✓let slip to me that. A pronoun object cannot follow slip: ✗let slip it, ✓let it slip.
entries.word order: both let slip that he was leaving and let it slip that he was leaving are standard; the second is commoner in speech, and the first slightly more literary.
entries.reports: revealing something by accident in the course of saying something else. Where blurt out is sudden and loud, let slip is quiet — the speaker often does not notice having done it.
entries.see also: blurt out, give away, let on, betray

examples: He finally owned up to sending the email.
Nobody owned up, so the whole class stayed late.
She owned up to her share of the mistake and no more.
It took him three days to own up to his father.
If you own up now, the fine is smaller.
He has never owned up to any part of it.
entries.pronunciation note: the to reduces to a schwa before a verb or a consonant
entries.русский: признаться, повиниться — разг.: сознаться в вине после попыток уйти от ответа
entries.patterns: own up (no complement) · own up + to + noun phrase · own up + to + -ing · own up + to sb · (literary, without the particle: own + that-clause)
entries.never: own up to do — the to is a preposition, so what follows it is a noun or an -ing form: ✗owned up to take the money, ✓owned up to taking the money. The that-clause is not available either: ✗He owned up that he had lied, ✓He owned up to lying, ✓He admitted that he had lied.
entries.the bare verb: own by itself once meant "admit," and it survives in formal writing — I own I was surprised, he owned himself beaten. It sounds deliberately old-fashioned now, and the phrasal own up to has taken over the ordinary work.
entries.reports: admitting fault after having tried not to. The evasion is presupposed — nobody owns up to something they were never hiding.
entries.see also: admit, confess, come clean, fess up

examples: She rebutted the charge point by point.
The defense had thirty minutes to rebut.
His letter rebuts the claim that the study was funded by the industry.
The presumption can be rebutted by documentary evidence.
Nobody at the hearing seriously rebutted the numbers.
The paper rebuts an argument that nobody had actually made.
entries.русский: возражать, приводить контрдоводы — юр., книжн.: отвечать на обвинение доводами
entries.patterns: rebut + noun phrase · rebut + the claim / charge / argument that · rebut (no complement, in debate) · passive be rebutted
entries.never: rebut that he was involved — no bare that-clause; the verb needs a noun phrase, and the claim that is the usual bridge: ✓rebutted the claim that he was involved. Also rebut to do, rebut -ing, and rebut me that.
entries.spelling: the t doubles before a vowel — rebutted, rebutting, rebuttal.
entries.reports: answering a charge with a counterargument. Where deny simply says no, rebut presupposes that reasons were given — and unlike refute it makes no claim that the reasons worked.

examples: The witness recanted on the second day of the trial.
He recanted his confession as soon as he had a lawyer.
She refused to recant anything she had written.
Two of the three signers later recanted.
The scientist was pressed to recant and would not.
Her earlier testimony was recanted but never struck from the record.
entries.русский: отречься от своих слов — книжн.: публично взять назад показания или убеждения
entries.type: reporting verb — withdrawal of a statement
entries.patterns: recant + noun phrase · recant (no complement) · passive be recanted
entries.never: recant that, recant -ing, recant to do, and recant me sth. ✗He recanted that he had seen her, ✓He recanted his statement, ✓He recanted.
entries.reports: publicly taking back something you had professed, usually under pressure and usually a belief, a confession, or testimony. Heavier than retract, which can apply to one sentence in a press release; recant keeps the weight of heresy trials and witness stands.

examples: The paper refutes the earlier finding with a much larger sample.
Nothing in the file refutes her account.
He believes he has refuted the objection; his critics disagree.
The claim was refuted within a day by the agency's own data.
She set out to refute the standard explanation and ended up confirming it.
A single receipt refuted the whole timeline.
entries.русский: опровергнуть — доказать ложность утверждения; не «отрицать», для этого deny
entries.patterns: refute + noun phrase · refute + the claim / allegation that · passive be refuted
entries.never: refute that he was involved — no bare that-clause. ✓refuted the allegation that he was involved; or, if a simple denial is what you mean, ✓denied that he was involved. Also refute to do, refute -ing, and refute me that.
entries.contested usage: in careful American usage refute means disprove — it says the counterargument succeeded. Press offices and headline writers routinely use it to mean deny, and the AP and most newsroom style guides tell them not to, because He refuted the charge announces that the charge is false rather than that he said so. The loose use is common enough that dictionaries now record it; it is still the kind of thing an editor changes.
entries.reports: proving a claim wrong. Use it only when you are prepared to endorse the result.

examples: The magazine retracted the story a week later.
He retracted the comment but not the sentiment behind it.
Two of her statements were retracted before the hearing.
The journal retracted the paper after the images were questioned.
She refused to retract a single word.
He retracted the accusation in open court.
entries.русский: отозвать, взять назад — офиц.: отказаться от сказанного или опубликованного
entries.type: reporting verb — withdrawal of a statement
entries.patterns: retract + noun phrase · passive be retracted
entries.never: retract that, retract -ing, retract to do, and retract me sth. ✗He retracted that he had said it, ✓He retracted the remark.
entries.reports: formally taking back something said or published. Lighter and more procedural than recant — a journal retracts a paper and a spokesman retracts a comment, and neither implies the change of heart that recant does.

examples: The interview revealed that she had been offered the job twice.
He never revealed who had told him.
The X-ray revealed a second fracture.
She revealed the plan to her staff an hour before the press got it.
It emerged later that the emails had been deleted — a detail no one had revealed at the time.
The documents reveal how the account was set up.
entries.русский: раскрыть, обнаружить — сообщить то, что до этого было скрыто
entries.patterns: reveal + that-clause · reveal + noun phrase · reveal + wh-clause · reveal + noun phrase + to sb · reveal + to sb + that-clause · reveal + oneself + as / to be · passive it was revealed that
entries.never: reveal me the truth — no double object; the recipient takes to: ✓revealed the truth to me, ✓revealed to me that. Also reveal to do and reveal -ing.
entries.reports: making known something that had been hidden. The concealment is presupposed, which is why revealed is unfair for a fact that was simply announced, and why a headline saying a study revealed a result oversells a study that merely found one.

examples: He spilled the details before I even asked.
Come on — spill.
She spilled the beans about the surprise party.
Somebody spilled everything to a reporter.
Two drinks in and he spilled the whole story.
Don't spill it before the announcement goes out.
entries.русский: выболтать, разболтать — разг.: охотно выдать секрет; spill the beans — проболтаться
entries.patterns: spill + noun phrase (the beans, the details, it, everything) · spill (no complement, as an invitation) · spill + noun phrase + to sb · spill + noun phrase + about + noun phrase (spill the beans about the party)
entries.never: spill that she was leaving — no that-clause; say spilled the news that she was leaving, or simply told everyone that she was leaving. Also spill to do, spill -ing, and spill me the details.
entries.the idiom: spill the beans is fixed — the beans never become anything else — and it is dated enough that plain spill has largely taken over in speech.
entries.reports: telling a secret readily, usually to someone who asked. No fault is presupposed, only a confidence broken, and the register is conversational throughout: it reads as slang in anything formal.
entries.see also: blurt out, give away, let slip, leak

entries.meaning: She suggested that he was at the meeting reports a claim about a fact; She suggested that he be at the meeting proposes an action. Only the proposal sense takes an -ing complement (suggested leaving), and it is the proposal sense that draws the American subjunctive.
examples: The timing suggests that somebody was warned in advance.
Are you suggesting that the numbers were changed?
Everything about the room suggested a hasty exit.
The evidence suggests he had been there before.
Her tone suggested that the conversation was over.
Nothing in the file suggests who approved the payment.
entries.pronunciation note: American English pronounces the /ɡ/; British English usually drops it, /səˈdʒɛst/
entries.русский: наводить на мысль, свидетельствовать — здесь о данных и уликах; значение «предлагать» — другое
entries.patterns: suggest + that-clause · suggest + noun phrase · suggest + wh-clause · suggest + to sb + that-clause · passive it is suggested that
entries.never: suggest someone to do something — suggest takes no personal object before its complement in either of its senses: ✗She suggested me to go, ✗She suggested him that he leave. Repairs: ✓She suggested that I go, ✓She suggested going, or switch verbs — ✓She advised me to go. Also suggest me that → ✓suggested to me that.
entries.two verbs in one spelling: the mood of the clause tells them apart.
entries.reports: evidence or wording pointing toward a conclusion without asserting it. Softer than imply, which points at an intention the speaker could have made explicit — a set of numbers can suggest something without meaning anything at all.

examples: The city unveiled its budget proposal on Tuesday.
They unveiled the memorial on the anniversary.
The company unveils a new phone every September.
The plan was unveiled at a press conference in Chicago.
She unveiled the design to a room of skeptical engineers.
Two agencies unveiled competing proposals in the same week.
entries.русский: представить, обнародовать — впервые публично показать вещь: продукт, план, памятник
entries.patterns: unveil + noun phrase · unveil + noun phrase + at / on / in · unveil + noun phrase + to sb · passive be unveiled
entries.never: unveil that, unveil -ing, unveil to do, and unveil sb sth. ✗The company unveiled that a new model was coming, ✓The company unveiled a new model.
entries.reports: showing something publicly for the first time. It takes a thing rather than a proposition — a product, a plan, a statue, a logo — which is exactly why no clause can follow it. Press releases have worn it thin; announce is the plainer verb and usually the more accurate one.

examples: She volunteered that she had seen the car twice that week.
He volunteered the information before anyone thought to ask for it.
Nobody volunteered anything useful about the schedule.
The witness volunteered that she had known the family for years.
He volunteered to me that the numbers had already been revised.
She volunteered nothing and answered only what she was asked.
entries.русский: сказать по своей инициативе — сообщить то, о чём никто не спрашивал
entries.patterns: volunteer + that-clause · volunteer + noun phrase · volunteer + noun phrase + to sb · volunteer + to sb + that-clause · (a different sense: volunteer + to-infinitive)
entries.never: volunteer me that → ✓volunteered to me that. Also volunteer -ing, and volunteer sb sth: ✗She volunteered us the information, ✓She volunteered the information to us.
entries.two senses: with a that-clause it reports speech nobody asked for (He volunteered that he'd been fired); with a to-infinitive it reports an offer to act (He volunteered to drive). Only the first is a reporting verb.
entries.reports: giving information that was not requested. The absence of a question is the whole meaning — you cannot volunteer an answer to something you were asked.
